Isaiah LaCombe Datasheet as part of Project X for Team 305

Submission: 3, 06, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the environmental sensor subsystem developed for our interplanetary rover. The purpose of this subsystem is to collect critical environmental data, including gas concentration, temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, and ambient light, and transmit it reliably to the rover’s communication network. The document outlines requirements, design decisions, and implementation details that guide the construction and verification of the subsystem as a modular, standalone PCB.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Our team designed the investigative rover as an open-ended exploration platform to simulate environmental monitoring on a planetary surface. The rover features modular subsystems, each responsible for a different function, such as sensing, actuation, HMI, and wireless communication. My module, the environmental sensor subsystem, focuses on collecting and transmitting environmental data through a UART daisy-chain network, enabling real-time telemetry to the base station or local display. This subsystem ensures that the rover can take precise sensor readings and safely navigate its environment while supporting the team’s mission objectives.

For full context of the team’s design concept and integrated rover system, see our team report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
I am responsible for designing, building, and verifying the environmental sensor subsystem. This includes:

  • Selecting and integrating a 4 in 1 sensor (gas, temperature, humidity, pressure)
  • Implementing UART communication for telemetry in the rover’s modular network
  • Designing the power system with a 3.3 V switching regulator and barrel jack input
  • Ensuring the subsystem is low-power, fail safe, and compatible with other team modules
  • Programming and debugging the microcontroller (PIC18F57Q43 48 Pin SMD)

To review detailed information about the components used in the subsystem, including sensor part numbers, microcontroller selection, and power considerations, see the "BOM" section of this datasheet. This helps anyone unfamiliar with the system understand exactly what materials and parts were used to implement this module.

docs.title: Project Requirements Description
docs.text:
The requirements table lists the functional, electrical, and interface constraints for the Environmental Sensor Subsystem of the interplanetary rover. This board is designed as a single, modular PCB responsible for collecting environmental data including gas concentration, temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, ambient light, and transmitting that data to the rover’s daisy-chained UART communication network.

The table below shows minimum and target performance levels to ensure the subsystem meets the team level design goals and course hardware constraints. These requirements will help with component selection, schematic design, firmware development, and system verification before integrating this subsystem with other rover boards.

docs.title: Other Useful Design Notes and Constraints
docs.text:
• Power Build: The board supports both bus power and a local 9 V barrel jack input, selectable using onboard jumpers as required by course specifications.
  • Power Budget: The environmental sensor subsystem is low-power by design, with total current draw expected to remain below 500 mA even during sensor warm-up and microcontroller peak usage.
  • Microcontroller: The subsystem supports either an ESP32 running MicroPython or a surface-mount PIC microcontroller, provided UART and I2C requirements are met.
  • Sensors: The subsystem integrates gas detection, temperature, humidity, pressure, and Light intensity.

docs.title: Module's Selected Major Components
docs.text:
The following sections describe the selected major components needed for the Environmental Monitoring Subsystem.

This subsystem:

  • Operates entirely at 3.3V with a 9V source
  • Measures gas concentration, temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure
  • Communicates sensor data digitally and analog to a microcontroller
  • Sends processed data to teammate boards via a 2×4 ribbon connector
  • all sensors are surface mount components

docs.title: Candidate 1 – MCP1700T-3302E/TT (Linear Regulator)
docs.text: Pros Cons Low cost Less efficient than switching Low dropout voltage Heat dissipation at higher input voltages Simple design Limited current output (250 mA)

docs.title: Candidate 2 – TLV70033 (Linear Regulator)
docs.text: Pros Cons Ultra-low quiescent current Slightly higher cost Stable 3.3V output Limited current (200 mA)

docs.title: Candidate 3 – LM2575T-3.3G (Switching Regulator)
docs.text: Pros Cons High efficiency More complex design Handles higher current Requires inductor + more components Less heat generation Higher cost

docs.title: Final Selection: LM2575T-3.3G
docs.text: Rationale: The system current requirements are within safe limits for a linear regulator. The MCP1700 provides sufficient current at low cost with minimal PCB complexity.

docs.title: Candidate 1 – MQ-135 (Analog Gas Sensor)
docs.text: Pros Cons Simple analog interface Requires calibration Widely documented Heater consumes significant current Low cost Lower precision Easy to prototype Analog noise possible

docs.title: Candidate 2 – CCS811 (Digital I2C Gas Sensor)
docs.text: Pros Cons Digital I2C interface More expensive Lower power consumption Requires initialization Integrated air quality algorithm Limited to air quality estimation Small footprint —

docs.title: Candidate 3 – BME680 (Gas + Temperature + Humidity + Pressure)
docs.text: Pros Cons Measures gas, temperature, humidity, and pressure More complex firmware Digital I2C interface Slightly higher cost Single integrated environmental sensor Requires sensor library Small footprint Gas output is resistance-based (requires interpretation)

docs.title: Final Selection – BME680
docs.text:
Rationale:

The BME680 was selected because it integrates four environmental sensors into a single device, allowing the system to measure gas resistance (air quality indicator), temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure using a single I²C interface. Using the BME680 significantly simplifies hardware design by eliminating the need for multiple discrete sensors and reducing the number of required microcontroller pins. Although the firmware implementation is slightly more complex, the integrated design results in a smaller PCB footprint, lower overall component count, and easier system integration.

Pros Cons Low cost Slower response Simple protocol Not fully surface mount friendly Moderate accuracy —

docs.title: Candidate 2 – SHT31 (I2C)
docs.text: Pros Cons High accuracy Higher cost Fully digital I2C — Surface mount package —

docs.title: Candidate 3 – HDC1080 (I2C)
docs.text: Pros Cons Low power Slightly lower accuracy than SHT31 Small footprint — Digital interface —

docs.title: Final Selection: SHT31
docs.text: Rationale: The SHT31 offers high accuracy, reliable I2C communication, and strong industry support while meeting surface mount requirements.

docs.title: Candidate 1 – BMP280
docs.text: Pros Cons Accurate readings Requires calibration constants Digital I2C — Low power —

docs.title: Candidate 2 – BME280 (Pressure + Temp + Humidity)
docs.text: Pros Cons Multi-function sensor Redundant if separate sensors used Compact Higher cost

docs.title: Candidate 3 – MPL3115A2
docs.text: Pros Cons Integrated altitude calculation Slightly higher cost Digital I2C —

docs.title: Final Selection: BMP280
docs.text: Rationale: The BMP280 provides accurate pressure readings with low power consumption and simple I2C integration while avoiding redundancy with separate temperature and humidity sensors.

docs.title: Microcontroller Selection
docs.text:
The microcontroller is responsible for:

  • Reading analog gas sensor data (ADC)
  • Communicating with digital sensors via I2C
  • Providing UART debugging interface
  • Driving LEDs and reading button input
  • Communicating with teammate boards via ribbon connector
  • Supporting ICSP programming

docs.title: Candidate 1 – PIC18F57Q43 (TQFP-40)
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Microchip

Pros Cons 12-bit ADC (ideal for analog gas sensor) 8-bit architecture Multiple I2C peripherals Less RAM than 32-bit MCUs Multiple UART modules No built-in wireless Large pin count (40 pins) — Supported in MPLAB X / Melody — Surface mount TQFP (easier than QFN) —

docs.title: Candidate 2 – PIC18F47Q10 (TQFP-40)
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Microchip

Pros Cons Lower cost than Q43 series Slightly fewer advanced peripherals Multiple ADC channels Lower ADC resolution (10-bit) Familiar architecture — Surface mount package —

docs.title: Candidate 3 – ESP32 (QFN)
docs.text:
Manufacturer: Espressif

Pros Cons 32-bit processor QFN package difficult to solder Built-in WiFi/BLE Overkill for subsystem High RAM Higher power consumption Multiple peripherals More complex firmware

docs.title: Final Selection: PIC18F57Q43
docs.text:
Rationale:

The PIC18F57Q43 provides:

  • 12-bit ADC resolution for accurate gas sensing
  • Multiple I2C modules for digital sensors
  • UART for debugging
  • Sufficient GPIO for LEDs and button
  • ICSP support for in-circuit programming
  • Surface-mount TQFP package that is practical for PCB assembly

It meets all subsystem requirements without adding unnecessary complexity or wireless overhead.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This subsystem interfaces with a BME680 environmental sensor using I2C and communicates with a 7-node daisy-chain UART network.

The subsystem is responsible for: - Reading environmental data (temperature, humidity, pressure, gas resistance) - Processing sensor data using calibration registers - Sending formatted UART messages to other subsystems - Receiving, processing, and forwarding UART messages in the daisy chain

Note: This subsystem does not generate unsolicited signals; it only transmits sensor data or acknowledgements for messages addressed to it.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: 7 subsystems connected in a UART daisy chain. Each subsystem: - Receives messages - Processes messages addressed to it - Forwards all other messages immediately and unchanged - Discards duplicate messages to prevent retransmission loops

docs.title: Sensor Interface (I2C)
docs.text: The BME680 is accessed via I2C.

docs.title: Message Types Used
docs.text: Message Type Description 8 Temperature Sensor Data Report 10 Barometric Pressure Data Report 11 Humidity Sensor Data Report 13 System Status Report 14 System Error Code Report 16 Heartbeat

docs.title: Message Definitions
docs.text:
Message Type 8 — Temperature Sensor Data Report

Byte Variable Name Type Min Max 1–2 message_type uint16_t 8 8 3–4 temperature int16_t -4000 8500

Temperature is scaled by 100 (°C × 100)

Message Type 10 — Pressure Data Report

Byte Variable Name Type Min Max 1–2 message_type uint16_t 10 10 3–6 pressure uint32_t 30000 110000 7–10 altitude int32_t -50000 100000

Message Type 11 — Humidity Data Report

Byte Variable Name Type Min Max 1–2 message_type uint16_t 11 11 3–4 humidity uint16_t 0 10000

Humidity is scaled by 100 (% × 100)

docs.title: Sensor Configuration
docs.text:
• Operating Mode: Forced Mode (trigger measurements on demand)
  • Oversampling: Improves measurement resolution (×1 to ×16 for T/P/H)
  • IIR Filter: Reduces temperature and pressure noise (coefficients 0–127)
  • Measurement Status Flags:
  • new_data → new measurement available
  • measuring → measurement in progress
  • gas_measuring → gas measurement in progress

docs.title: I2C Communication Details
docs.text:
• Slave address: 0x76 or 0x77 (depends on SDO pin)
  • Supports Start, Stop, repeated start, auto-increment reads
  • Soft reset: 0xB6 to 0xE0

docs.title: Incoming Message Handling
docs.text:
1. Check message validity: proper frame, correct length, valid type
  2. Check sender: discard if from this subsystem
  3. Check destination:
  4. If addressed to this subsystem → process & send ACK
  5. Else → forward unchanged
  6. Duplicate messages: discard to prevent loops

docs.title: Forwarding Behavior
docs.text:
• Immediate forwarding for all non-local messages
  • Prioritized over new transmissions

docs.title: Acknowledgement Message
docs.text: Byte Variable Name Type Description 1–2 message_type uint16_t Type of received message 3 received_msg uint8_t Original message ID 4 status uint8_t 1 → success, 0 → error

docs.title: Sender Behavior
docs.text:
• Periodically transmit sensor readings: temperature, pressure, humidity
  • Messages must be formatted, payload ≤ limits, dynamically updated
  • Transmission controlled by a non-blocking timer
  • Data packed as scaled integers for reliable UART transmission

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text:
The Environmental Monitoring Subsystem operates entirely from a single regulated 3.3V power rail generated by a switching regulator.

This power budget verifies that:

  • All major components are accounted for
  • The 3.3V regulator can supply sufficient current
  • The external 9V source can support the regulator
  • A 25% safety margin is included

docs.title: Section A – Major Components and Maximum Current
docs.text:
The following major components require power.

Component Operating Voltage Absolute Max Current (mA) Notes PIC18F57Q43 3.3V 48 mA Worst-case active operation MQ-135 Gas Sensor (heater + analog circuit) 3.3V 150 mA Heater is dominant load SHT31 Temp/Humidity Sensor 3.3V 2 mA During measurement BMP280 Pressure Sensor 3.3V 1 mA Peak measurement BH1750 Light Sensor 3.3V 1 mA Peak measurement Red LED 3.3V 10 mA GPIO current limited Blue LED 3.3V 10 mA GPIO current limited UART Header (logic-level load) 3.3V 5 mA Estimated external load

docs.title: Section B – Power Rail Assignment
docs.text: All components operate on a single 3.3V power rail.

docs.title: Section C – Voltage Regulator Selection
docs.text: Because the system requires approximately 284 mA worst-case, a switching regulator is preferred over a linear regulator to minimize thermal dissipation when stepping down from 9V to 3.3V.

docs.title: Candidate 1 – LM2575-3.3G (Switching Regulator)
docs.text:
• Output Voltage: 3.3V
  • Maximum Output Current: 1A
Pros Cons High efficiency (~75–80%) Requires inductor and diode 1A output (large safety margin) Larger PCB footprint Low heat dissipation Slightly more complex design Well-documented reference designs —

docs.title: Candidate 2 – MCP1700-3302 (Linear Regulator)
docs.text:
• Output Voltage: 3.3V
  • Maximum Output Current: 250 mA
Pros Cons Simple implementation Insufficient current capability (after margin) Low cost Significant heat dissipation at 9V input Small SOT-23 package No margin for heater load

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The MCP1700 cannot reliably supply the required 284 mA including safety margin.

The LM2575 provides up to 1A output current and significantly improved efficiency when stepping down from 9V to 3.3V. This minimizes thermal stress and ensures stable operation when the gas sensor heater and microcontroller are active simultaneously.

Regulator Selected for 3.3V Rail: LM2575-3.3G Switching Regulator

docs.title: Selected Source
docs.text: 9V DC Wall Adapter Rated Current: 3A

docs.title: Worst-Case Output Power (3.3V Rail)
docs.text:
Using required current including safety margin:

P_out = 3.3V × 0.284A P_out ≈ 0.94 W

Assuming 80% regulator efficiency:

P_in = 0.94W / 0.80 P_in ≈ 1.18 W

docs.title: Input Current from 9V Supply
docs.text:
I_in = 1.18W / 9V I_in ≈ 0.13 A

Approximately 130 mA drawn from the 9V adapter (worst case)

docs.title: External Supply Margin Check
docs.text:
Adapter Rating: 3.0 A Required Current: 0.13 A

Remaining Current = 3.0A − 0.13A = 2.87 A

  • External supply easily supports subsystem
  • No negative current margin
  • Substantial available headroom

docs.title: Section E – Battery Life Calculation
docs.text:
Not applicable.

This subsystem is powered by a regulated 9V wall adapter and is not battery-operated.

If converted to battery operation in the future:

Battery Life (hours) = Battery Capacity (mAh) / Total Current (mA)

Example using a 500 mAh battery:

500 mAh / 284 mA ≈ 1.76 hours

This runtime would be insufficient for long-term deployment, further justifying the selection of a wall-powered supply.

docs.title: Final Power System Summary
docs.text:
Power Rail Voltage Required Current (with Margin) Regulator Rail 1 3.3V 300 mA LM2575-3.3G

The selected regulator and 9V power adapter provide sufficient current capacity, appropriate safety margin, and improved thermal performance for continuous operation of the Environmental Monitoring Subsystem.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This schematic is designed to support the environmental Sensor Subsystem Board. It regulates a DC 9V wall adapter input down to 3.3V using an LM2575T-3.3G switchiung regulator with diode and fuse protection. The 3.3V rail powers a PIC18F57Q43 48 pin microcontroller that monitors a all in 1 temperature, humidity, pressure, and gas monitoring sensor. The system provides stable sensor inputs, onboard filtering, expansion Pins, and a ribbon connector for inter-board communication.”
